Name: Aaron Davis
Question: What is the difference between anachronism and time jumping (flashback and flashforward) in literature?
Answer: Anachronism is a factual error in the portrayal of a time period. What you’re calling “time jumping” is simply showing the same work at different in-universe times. I’m going to show you a film with examples of both. The excellent film A Knight's Tale is deliberately and gleefully anachronistic in many respects. It's a modern-style sports movie with a classic rock soundtrack and a romantic comedy subplot… that happens to be set in late 14th century France during the Hundred Years’ War, and the sport is jousting. The film is loosely based on the first story from Geoffrey Chaucer’s anthology The Canterbury Tales, depicting an English yeoman, William Thatcher (played by the late Heath Ledger), trying to rise above his common roots and become a knight. To that end, he squires for a poor knight named Sir Ector for almost nine years, then Sir Ector suddenly dies of a heart attack while trying to take a crap between bouts. William and his fellow servants Roland (Mark Addy) and Wat (Alan Tudyk), penniless and starving, dress William in Ector’s armor and have him finish the joust so they can eat and get home on the prize money. And they come on to the tournament pitch to the tune of “We Will Rock You” by Queen, released in 1977. The sequence was originally filmed as a joke, but they decided it was so awesome afterwards that they left it in the final cut of the film. The justification they gave for using a classic rock soundtrack in a film about jousting was to show the audience that medieval people thought their music was just as cool as we think ours is. But this is far from the only anachronism in the film: for example, the majority of the clothing worn by William’s love interest Lady Jocelyn (Shannyn Sossamon) is completely inaccurate to how a typical 14th century Anglo-French noblewoman would have dressed. Yeah, showing her cleavage under sheer gauze to her navel? Not a thing. You’re more likely to get an off-the-shoulder button-front dress like this. Later in the film, we get a couple of flashbacks, for example this one depicting William’s father John taking him across the English Channel to meet Sir Ector for the first time.

Question: Would the clone troopers obeyed order 66, if they weren’t fitted with inhibitor chips?
Answer: Most would, some wouldn't. Which, believe it or not, is exactly what happened in the Legends continuity, where there were no inhibitor chips. The inhibitor chips were wholly an invention of the Clone Wars TV series, which de facto de-canonized the entire Clone Wars Multimedia Project long before the Disney takeover. Before that, in Legends, the clones made up their own minds. Believe it or not, this question speaks to a very real and important topic in military ethics: the duty to disobey an unlawful order. You see, in Western common law, there’s a longstanding tradition that the rules and regulations of the organization and the state take precedence over the wishes of any superior, even a King. Exhibit A: the Magna Carta, which the nobility of England forced King John Plantagenet to sign in 1215. While its actual effectiveness is debatable, it is often credited as introducing the concept of “rule of law”, rather than “rule of man”. If even a King is not above the law, then it logically follows that a King can give orders which are illegal, and therefore are not to be followed. Arguably the most famous expression of this happened in the post-World War II era at the Nuremberg war crimes tribunals, where the defense counsels of high-ranking officers of Hitler’s regime were banned by the court from using the so-called defense of superior orders, but it’s been around in fits and starts for centuries. I explore it in greater detail in this answer: Here’s where theory and practice collide, however: soldiers are trained to follow orders. Questioning orders isn’t something armies generally like, for reasons that should be fairly obvious. So, while ideally we would like a soldier to immediately refuse an order that is unlawful, in practice a soldier who receives an unlawful order often won’t even consider the lawfulness of an order, especially while keyed-up on adrenaline during combat or when an authority figure they generally trust gives it. It was for this reason that, contrary to popular belief, the post-WWII war crimes trials tended to cut more slack to more junior personnel: they were viewed as so dominated by their superiors that it was reasonable that, barring evidence to the contrary, they were assumed to not have been able to tell whether what they were doing was unlawful. In Star Wars, we further learned in Attack of the Clones that the Kaminoans genetically modified their slave soldiers to be less capable of independent thought than their baseline human donor, Jango Fett. Add to that a decade of highly regimented training and indoctrination, and you get a slave army that, while more able to improvise when things go wrong than the remote-controlled drones used by the Trade Federation et al., is not that capable of thinking for itself whether the orders they’re given are lawful. Which is fitting, considering that the very existence of a slave army is itself unlawful in the Republic. So what ended up happening is that most of the slaves received a “break glass in case of fire” order from their commander-in-chief—which Karen Traviss’s Republic Commando novel series not-unreasonably interpreted as part of a list of over 150 such orders,[1]because this is how such things tend to work in real military forces—and just obeyed what they believed to be a lawful order to frag their overseers. This was the explanation used in Matthew Stover’s much-loved Revenge of the Sith novelization. It’s also why the Jedi had so little warning despite their precognition: the slaves, by and large, bore little to no malice towards their overseers. They simply received what appeared to be a valid order, and obeyed it. With the Jedi Order overextended, spread thin across the galaxy, each Jedi is alone, surrounded only by whatever clone troops he, she, or it commands. War itself pours darkness into the Force, deepening the cloud that limits Jedi perception. And the clones have no malice, no hatred, not the slightest ill intent that might give warning. They are only following orders. In this case, Order Sixty-Six. Hold-out blasters appear in clone hands. ARC-170s drop back onto the tails of Jedi starfighters. AT-STs swivel their guns. Turrets on hovertanks swung silently. Clones open fire, and Jedi die. All across the galaxy. All at once. Jedi die.[2] But that isn’t the whole story in Legends. You see, not all the slaves were alike: while thinking critically was discouraged by the Kaminoans, it still had to be present to allow the slaves to “think creatively”. This was especially true of the higher-grade slaves: the clone commandos and the elite ARC Troopers. And this meant that contact with reality meant some slaves did think about it, especially when their Jedi overseers weren’t immediately at hand to shoot at (meaning more time to consider things). And they didn’t all come to the same conclusions. So again, the answer is: Most did, but some didn’t.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Which antagonists were not villains?
Answer: Jim Trotter III. Jim Trotter (played by Lane Smith) is the prosecutor for the State of Alabama in the 1992 legal comedy My Cousin Vinny. He spends the movie working to convict Bill Gambini and Stan Rothenstein, two college students from New York, of the murder of a convenience store clerk. They didn’t do it, and they hire Bill’s eponymous cousin Vinny Gambini, a personal injury lawyer by trade, to get them off. Unlike what happens in a lot of Hollywood legal thrillers, or in such things as the Ace Attorney franchise, Jim Trotter is not a malicious or villainous figure. He’s not railroading the boys to maintain a perfect record or anything, he’s just a professional doing his frickin’ job in the Anglo-American common law system: he presents his case against Gambini and Rothenstein and sees if the defense can knock it apart. He has to prove that they did do it, within the law, and does his best given the evidence in his possession. And while Vinny doesn’t have to prove they didn’t commit the crime, once Trotter is shown beyond any doubt that the police pulled over the wrong car, he immediately moves to dismiss the charges himself. No harm, no foul. Not for nothing is this film a favorite of real-life legal professionals: everything in it can and does happen in real-life courtrooms.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: Do heavy metal bands use backing tracks for their live shows?
Answer: Frequently. This is frankly kind of routine these days. Especially in subgenres like power and melodic metal that use a lot of synth, it’s common for all that to be on a backing track. And it could be as simple as the band not having enough people in it to play all the instruments they want. Powerwolf is a good example. They have a full-time keyboardist, but Charles Greywolf is both the band’s rhythm guitarist and bassist, and tracks the bass for their live performances. This was an intentional decision according to frontman Attila Dorn: they decided as a band that they have a good thing going and don’t want to risk screwing up the interpersonal balance of the group by adding a touring bassist. Sabaton, on the other hand, decided not to get a new keyboardist after Daniel Mÿhr left in 2012. Frontman Joakim Brodén started as a keyboardist (his first instrument was a Hammond B3 organ in fact), and sometimes breaks out a keyboard for certain songs (“The Red Baron” and “Christmas Truce” in particular), but for the most part he’s running around the stage too much. The synth is part of their sound but not the core of it, so tracking it is a good solution. Bloodywood has several multi-instrumentalists in the studio and touring bands, but if they wanted to play everything live they’d practically need an orchestra. So depending on the song, lead guitarist Karan Katiyar will play either a guitar or a flute, Sarthak Pahwa usually plays a dhol or another instrument, and they track the rest. On the other hand, you have groups like Nightwish, where keyboardist Tuomas Holopainen is the core of the sound. They do use tracks, but it’s all manually controlled by him from his triple Korg keyboards: he’s typically playing with one hand and programming with another because he’s just that damn good at it and nitnoid about it. Metal isn’t all one thing. Its diversity is what makes it fun.

Question: Could you "program in pure machine code" by manually writing out bytecode in a .bin file and then running it? If it's of any importance, I'm using Ubuntu Linux. Would this work?
Answer: Sure. Why would you want to? This an MSP430 development board from Texas Instruments, similar to the one I’ve used in class at NC A&T. It has a 16-bit ARM microcontroller in it that you program with the Micro USB port in the upper-right corner and TI’s IDE, Code Composer Studio. Now, you can’t write straight-up machine code for this using the standard methods, but you can do the next best thing: assembly language. This is the level of programming that the IDE converts into machine code. Alternatively, you can write in a high-level programming language, namely C (the 1989 standard by default; you can also use the 1999 or 2014 standards with some adjustments). High-level programming languages are representations of assembly language, which your coding environment compiles into assembly language and then assembles into machine code. This is a very simple program to procedurally divide one number by another number using C, reading the memory using the development environment. I had to do this for a lab assignment in my Introduction to Microprocessors class. This is the equivalent program in MSP430 assembly language. See how much longer that is? Each one of those lines of assembly language equates to a single instruction in machine code, and even discounting the stuff off the top and bottom that were included in TI’s assembly template (lines 1–25 and 58–68), it’s still more than twice as long as the C program. And even here, it’s still somewhat legible: you can see, for example, that I’m doing some arithmetic (e.g. add, dec), that I’m doing some jumps (jge, jmp), and designating some memory space for variables (Dn: .short 40). In-line comments certainly help but they’re not that necessary. Now, these are some machine language instructions for the ARM processor architecture that this MCU is based on. It’s pretty common nowadays: most major chipmakers for embedded systems use it. I copied these straight out of the machine code from my Computer Architecture professor. Good luck with that one, brother. I passed the test on reading these and I still couldn’t tell you what they actually meant without the handout in front of me. In order they are: Seriously, folks, we invented high-level programming languages for a reason: it’s way, way easier than raw machine code. So, yes, you could write raw machine code for a Ubuntu Linux machine, but unless you’re a professional computer architecture engineer and/or a masochist, there’s no actual reason within twelve parsecs of Sanity Street why you would ever want to. Question: If you had been given free reign over The Clone Wars by George Lucas himself (no limits), how would you have written it out?
Answer: I’m going to begin with the assumption that the start and end points have to be basically the same as the original timeline (OTL). In which case, this is the major change I’d make, because it’s my major beef with the way the conflict is presented in canon. Have the Jedi address the sins of the Republic. The Republic in the prequels is comically corrupt and evil, as I’ve discussed in multiple previous answers. This is driven home by the fact that they literally bought and paid for a billions-strong slave army, violating their own stated laws against slavery, because they couldn’t stand the idea that people might want to say “fuck this shit, I’m out”. And the Jedi in canon unquestioningly support this policy. The only ones that don’t, get smeared as dirty stinkin’ Sith or the equivalent. Lookin’ at you, Barriss Offee. And yet we’re still expected to accept that the Republic and the Jedi are the good guys even though they systematically deny basic human rights to billions. You want to know how you present the Jedi and the Republic sympathetically here? Show us the Jedi and the Republic being heroic. Chopping brainless droids in half is easy. Real courage, real morality, is when you hold your own side accountable. So. Show them near-universally reacting with genuine horror at the mere concept of the clone army: not those half-assed "being nice to your slaves" scenes we actually got from Plo Koon et al. in TCW, but actively acknowledging that they are slaves and doing something about it. Show real internal debate over whether they should even be involved with the Republic anymore at all. Show Jedi quitting the Order over it as conscientious objectors, like Bardan Jusik did in the Republic Commando novels, and not turning into bomb-throwing terrorists, Inquisitors, or Sith. “So how do we justify what we are doing now? Breeding men without choice, and without freedom, to fight and die for us? When do the means cease to justify the end? Where is our society heading? Where are our ideals, and what are we without them? If we give in to expedience in this way, where do we draw the line between ourselves and those we find unacceptably evil? I have no answer, Masters. Do you?”[1] And show us others deciding to work internally to try to change minds and mitigate and repair the damage. Hell, one of the main cast members is literally an ex-slave himself and is married to a senator. Instead of leaving Anakin Skywalker’s enslavement as a cheap trick to inspire sympathy for his childhood self, show Anakin and Padmé talking about how wrong this is. Show Padmé sponsoring legislation to emancipate the clones and compensate them for their enslavement. While we’re at it, have her propose sanctioning the Kaminoans for their participation and direct the Republic Judiciary to begin investigating them for crimes against civilization—because according to Lama Su in Attack of the Clones, this isn’t even the first clone army they've made. Obi-Wan Kenobi: Master Sifo-Dyas was killed almost ten years ago. Lama Su: Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that. But I'm sure he would have been proud of the army we've built for him. Obi-Wan: The army? Lama Su: Yes, a clone army. And, I must say, one of the finest we've ever created.[2] You can still have the same endpoint, and it makes Sidious’s victory an even bigger tragedy than before: now the biochipped clones don’t gun down their slave overseers, but rather the people who were actively trying to make them whole. Lucasfilm did none of that, before or after Disney. They just told us the Jedi were “the good guys” and “had no choice”. Just like Lando “had no choice” but to betray Han on Cloud City. Remember what Leia and Chewbacca thought of that excuse? Sorry about the fan edit, I couldn’t find the original clip. Out here in the real world, one of the fundamental principles of the rule of law is that a superior, no matter if they’re a sergeant, a butterbar lieutenant, a general, or the President of the godsdamned United States, cannot arbitrarily order you to violate the law purely on their own say-so. It’s not allowed, and cannot be allowed. And this isn’t even a new idea: it’s existed in the common law since the 1400s at least. And it’s not a foreign idea to science fiction, either. Exhibit A: Star Trek. Exhibit B: Babylon 5. But apparently George Lucas and Dave Filoni never got that memo. In one movie they talk up the Republic’s antislavery laws, and in the next the entire Republic’s governing structure, Jedi and all, nods along approvingly as billions of slaves march into ships to fight their war for them. Simply put, in Attack of the Clones and The Clone Wars, Lucas and Filoni took “the guardians of peace and justice in the Old Republic”, and turned them into villains as bad as Sith: they took the “quicker, easier, more seductive” route of simply bowing their heads and nodding along when tyranny gave them their marching orders. At least Sheev Palpatine never pretended he was the hero, not to the audience.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: In Star Trek, what would happen if someone surrendered to the Klingons during the Kobayashi Maru test or asked the Klingons to help them rescue the crew instead of attempting the rescue mission?
Answer: They’d lose. The computer simulation is designed to alter the parameters of the test so that you always fail. The point of the test is not to have the officer candidate being tested succeed. The point of the test is to judge their character: see how they handle themselves under pressure, test their problem-solving capabilities, and see how they react to a scenario where they’re destined to fail no matter what they do.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: In your opinion, what was the most visually stunning and emotional fight you've seen in anime?
Answer: Oliver Horn and Nanao Hibiya v. Vera Miligan, Reign of the Seven Spellblades episode 6, “Arise”. Oliver and Nanao, who matriculated to Kimberly Magic Academy less than a month ago, confront fourth-year student Vera Miligan, who turns out to be the culprit behind most of the mayhem of the previous five episodes and has kidnapped their friend Katie. Oliver and Nanao are already thought to be the two best fighters in their year after the events of episode 4, but Miligan easily holds them both off at once: she’s amused by their efforts, while Oliver and Nanao are fighting for their lives and the unconscious Katie’s.* The fight choreography is simply spectacular. There’s not a single wasted movement from any of the participants, the light shows from spells going off never block your view of the action, and it completely sells the fact that Oliver and Nanao have their work cut out for them. Oliver’s abilities as a strategist are on full display, and Nanao’s instincts as a swordswoman and growth as a mage allow for some surprises that will become trademarks for her as the series goes on. * Admittedly, Miligan says she planned to return Katie unharmed, but only after doing some nonconsensual exploratory surgery on Katie’s brain.

Question: Do you just allow your players to multi-class, if your particular TTRPG allows, or do you require some sort of in-game explanation/justification?
Answer: Yes. When I’m running Pathfinder, multiclassing is completely allowed. In-universe explanations are encouraged but not required. One of our players has made a Bard/Swashbuckler in two of the three campaigns we’ve played (first a heavily Dark Souls and Garth Nix-influenced dark fantasy campaign in Golarion, and currently War for the Crown). Although he’s got a straight Zen Archer prepared for our next one, which I’m running. One of the other PCs in that campaign plans to start as an Unarmed Fighter and then immediately jump to Oracle. His character is a “blind monk” archetype, with a seeing-eye dog; the fighter dip is for the bonus feats. The campaign in between, the bardbuckler player was the GM, and I was playing a Freebooter/Pistolero. Mona Wearn was a privateer-turned-pirate with a very, very deep connection to the ocean: she was a half-elf, and I liked to joke that the other half was fish. And she loved guns almost as much as she loved swimming and sailing. I built her to be extremely dangerous at short distances, with dual swords as a backup for four pistols: fully buffed, she could easily lay down 100 damage a round by the end of the campaign, while having a base AC of 28 between Dex, armor, and magic items.

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: What rules, references, or books do you still use from past editions of gaming rules like D&D or Pathfinder? What would you recommend to others even though they’re no longer in wide use?
Answer: One of the nice things about running Pathfinder First Edition is that, in addition to the wide selection of Paizo's own books to draw from, you can pull in the even bigger selection of D&D Third and 3.5 Edition books with very little statblock rewriting. There’s a few specific 3.5E books that I’ve dug out of my collection for the needs of my specific campaign (Lost Empires of Faerûn for one[1]), but if you want recommendations of a few that are more broadly usable, then let’s start with The Draconomicon. This is one of the biggest books that Wizards ever printed during Third Edition. Seriously, it’s thicc. This is a setting-agnostic book that contains everything you could ever possibly want to know about the second half of the name “Dungeons & Dragons” and then some: not just statblocks and quick blurbs, but extended essays on dragons’ biology, life cycles, mating and childrearing habits, what individual species like and don’t like, how they think, how they interact, you name it. Even if you never roll a single d20 with any of the statblocks in this book,* the information in it is indispensable for running dragon-related adventures. * Some of which are actually really cool: there’s a couple of prestige classes for dragons (one good, one evil) that let you give a level of a divine spellcasting class to a dragon and then treat the dragon’s effective levels of sorcerer from its age as extra levels of the divine class instead. Second, The Book of Exalted Deeds and The Book of Vile Darkness. These two books together (as well as their Forgotten Realms-specific counterparts Champions of Valor and Champions of Ruin) contain some of the better musings on the fundamental nature of the forces of Good and Evil, and what it means to be good or evil in the context of D&D. For example, it makes the argument that a truly Good character needs to be actively trying to do good: a character who merely talks about all the evil things they haven’t done is Neutral at best. They also explicitly point out that a paladin is supposed to default to the Good over the Law if they’re caught in a situation where the two are in conflict. There are admittedly a few things in them that didn’t age well (The Book of Vile Darkness has a bit of a hard-on for BDSM, and The Book of Exalted Deeds has “they’re mind-control drugs BUT THEY’RE TOTALLY GOOD, OKAY?!”), but overall they still mostly hold up. Third, Faiths of Eberron. Most Dungeons & Dragons settings have a very simplistic view of religion, in that there is only one of them: polytheism. Worshiping one god versus worshiping another god is a matter of personal preference: you still fundamentally accept that all the gods are real, you just have one or more in particular that you like better than the others. The Eberron setting, which was first officially published during 3.5E, is very different. Multiple entirely separate and mutually contradictory religions exist, much like in the real world where the Abrahamic faiths (which all claim to worship the same god, even if they claim the other two are doing it wrong) exist alongside Hinduism and Shintoism, neopagan faiths like Wicca and Asatru, and many still-extant indigenous faiths. Similarly in Eberron, the basic D&D polytheist faith of the Sovereign Host and Dark Six exists alongside the henotheistic Silver Flame faith, the Blood of Vol mystery cult which claims the only divinity exists within mankind itself, the fully atheistic quori Paths, and the ancestor worship of the isle of Aerenal. As a consequence of which, this book contains some of the better philosophical takes on the fundamental nature of religion—what it actually means to be a religious person beyond treating your divine patron as a vending machine for cool powers—that Wizards ever published. Understanding how religion works in your world is, I think, a very important worldbuilding concern: if a priest has real, measurable power—as indeed they do in most D&D worlds—then where does that power come from? And can that power be removed if you displease your patron? If you talk to God, does God talk back? Or are priests really just a weird kind of wizard and the gods aren’t actually real?

Name: Aaron Davis
Question: I bought a 10 year old car with 13 year old tires from a used car dealership and just found out. What, if any, legal action should I take?
Answer: None. This is why you do pre-purchase inspections. I've never owned a vehicle younger than five years old, and most were a lot older than that (my current record-holder is a 1974 Honda CB750). If you bought a car that old, there's almost certainly no warranty: any reasonable person would expect you to know that you're buying the car as-is. That's why you take the car over to your own regular mechanic to have them find everything that's wrong with it before you fork over a single red cent. Some more reputable used car lots, like Sanford Imports where I bought my current 2015 Chevy Equinox, will offer a dealer warranty to fix problems that crop up within a short time of purchase (the dealer fixed a bad axle seal and replaced the rear tires on the Equinox for free, both found by my mechanic before I bought it), but beyond that you're on your own. Furthermore, tires are consumables. Any reasonable person would expect them to wear out and need to be periodically replaced. And tires can be pricey so if the used car lot touched them at all, they probably put on the cheapest rubber they could find. Frankly, you'll probably pay less to just take the L and have new tires put on the car yourself than you would to any lawyer willing to take this case.

Question: How much better is the Gerald R Ford class of aircraft carriers over the preceding Nimitz class?
Answer: Incremental improvement. The two ships are structurally almost indistinguishable, aside from the Ford-class dropping an elevator that was never used underway anyway. The main difference is the electromagnetic aircraft launch system (EMALS) replacing steam catapults. It’s basically a railgun with a plane hooked to it. These have many fewer moving parts, meaning significant improvements in mechanical reliability. In other words, you're a lot less likely to get into a situation like what happened in the final battle of Top Gun where both catapults broke down at a critical moment, making it impossible for the Enterprise to launch any reinforcements after they sent up Maverick and Merlin. Skip to 2:40. Admittedly, this is deliberately a nightmare scenario brought on by a contrived coincidence of Hollywood, and therefore extremely unlikely in real life, but eliminating possible failure points is never a bad thing. The more common advantage of EMALS is significantly better control over launch acceleration curves: in other words, they can very precisely customize the boost to the aircraft and weather conditions. Steam catapults can't do this: they go at whatever speed they go at. Apart from EMALS, the main improvement over the Nimitz is an increase in automation, which cuts crew costs.
